catalog_quote: All Segai-Modang languages have strong word-final stress, an areal feature of the part of Borneo where these languages are found. Many of the sound changes that have affected Segai-Modang are motivated by this strong stress. Some of these changes can be found in more distantly related languages, and it is necessary to ensure that convergence is ruled out in sound changes which are claimed to define the group. The following tables provide a list of reflexes of PMP phonemes in four Segai-Modang languages, Modang (of the Kalinjau river), Long Gelat, Gaai, and Kelai, with discussion after. [...] [fn. 7, p. 76:] The term “sesquisyllabic” indicates a canonical word shape of a short unstressed initial syllable with reduced vowels and a long stressed final syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls invariably on the final syllable (strong, fixed, non-contrastive); words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic (Cə)ˈCV(ː)(C), with the prefinal syllable reduced to unstressed schwa.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Modang (words are at most sesquisyllabic).
new_statements.exceptions: None. Corroborated independently by Revel-Macdonald 1982:324 for the Long Bentuk and Nehes Liah Bing dialects ('Stress being fixed is not relevant and the strong accentuation on the last syllable weakens the first syllable') and restated in Smith 2019 (OL 58: 353, and sec. 7: 'regular word-final stress of the modern languages').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on elicited lexical items (c. 1,000-item vocabularies, citation forms) from Smith's 2015-16 fieldwork at Woq Helaq (Kelinjau Modang) and Long Gelat; stress described impressionistically as 'strong', no instrumental data; phrase-level prosody not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Smith's primary Modang data are from the Kelinjau-river dialect (Woq Helaq / Mei Lan; Glottolog keli1252 'Kelingan') and from Long Gelat (long1405 'Long Glat'), both Glottolog dialects of moda1244; his stress sentence is stated generically for all Segai-Modang languages and therefore also covers Segai (sega1243: Gaai, Kelai, Wahau). Revel-Macdonald 1982 describes the Long Bentuk (long1404) and Nehes Liah Bing (liah1237, = Wehea) dialects, also under moda1244 (Smith 2019 suggests Wahau/Wehea patterns with Segai).

sources.citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2019. A reconstruction of Proto-Segai-Modang. Oceanic Linguistics 58(2): 353-385. doi:10.1353/ol.2019.0012 (author-hosted proof PDF)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Abstract p. 353: 'Segai-Modang languages are stress-final and have innovated sesqui- and monosyllabic canonical word forms'; sec. 1: PSM 'schwa was the only penultimate vowel and stress was on the ultima', canonical shape *(Cə)ˈCV(ː)(C); sec. 7 (proof p. 26): 'It follows from the sesquisyllabic word-shape and regular word-final stress of the modern languages that PSM stress was also word-final.' Data from six varieties incl. Mei Lan, Woq Helaq, Long Gelat (Modang).

sources.note: p. 324 (Long Bentuk and Nehes Liah Bing dialects, 1977 fieldwork): 'The evolution of Modang seems to be linked with the weight of the final articulation. It is demonstrated at the phonic level by two characteristics, namely stress and length. Stress being fixed is not relevant and the strong accentuation on the last syllable weakens the first syllable, and by so doing has probably tended to erase it completely.' I.e. fixed, non-contrastive final stress.
